Admit, anchor, reason. Say what you don't know in one sentence without apologizing, name the nearest thing you do know, then reason out loud from it: “I haven't used X, but it solves the same problem as Y, so I'd expect…, and I'd confirm it by…”.
Name the gap precisely. Separate a forgotten detail (a method name) from a missing concept, and a fact to verify from a design choice.
State the consequence of being wrong. If a repeated call could duplicate a charge, the unknown matters; if it only affects a label, move on. This shows prioritization.

Proceed under a labeled assumption with a fallback: “assuming requests carry an idempotency key; otherwise I'd use…”. Keep it visible, and revise when the interviewer corrects it. Do not assume away the very thing being tested.
Say how you would verify: which source or experiment, and what result would change your decision. “I'd Google it” says nothing.
Use hints. Repeat the hint back and update your reasoning.
If there is no bridge at all, say so and offer to reason from first principles or return to it later.

Pointwise: score one answer against a rubric (1–5, or pass/fail per criterion).
Pairwise: pick the better of two answers (A/B). More stable than absolute scores, but costs two calls to remove order effects.
Reference-guided: the judge also sees a gold answer or the retrieved context, and checks the answer against it.
p_oobserved agreement between judge and human
p_eagreement expected if both labeled at random with their own label frequencies
Human ceiling: measure agreement between two humans on the same items. The judge cannot reasonably be expected to exceed it.
Agreement where it matters: compute agreement on the items where the two versions under test differ. High overall agreement can hide failures on exactly those items.
Per segment: by question type, answer length, and difficulty.
Bias probes: run the quick tests in the previous table and record the results.
Uncertainty: bootstrap a confidence interval for agreement and for score differences between versions; a small gain on a few hundred items is often noise.
Judge change control: re-score the calibration set whenever the judge model, rubric, or sampling settings change, and require a minimum agreement before using it.
Sharpen the rubric. Separate criteria (correctness, groundedness, completeness, conciseness), define each score level, and state that length is not quality and that unnecessary length is penalized.
Score per criterion before the overall score. Ask for a short reason and the criterion scores, then the verdict. This reduces the halo effect of one strong impression.
Give the judge evidence. Supply the retrieved context or a reference answer so it checks claims rather than guessing.
Add few-shot examples from the human-labeled set, including cases where the longer or more fluent answer is worse.
Control order and noise. In pairwise mode, run both orders and keep the verdict only when they agree, otherwise call it a tie. Use temperature 0, or average several samples.
Control length. Compare at matched length, regress score on length and use the residual, or penalize length beyond a target explicitly.
Use a different model family from the system under test, and consider an ensemble of two judges that must agree.

Fine-tune only if agreement is still low and you have enough labeled data. Supervised fine-tuning on human labels, or a trained reward model, is the usual route. Direct preference optimization (DPO) trains a generator on preference pairs and is a less direct fit for a scoring model; a small set of spot checks also risks overfitting.

Load balancing spreads requests across existing backends — Kubernetes Service / ingress (nginx, Envoy, cloud load balancer), or Ray Serve’s router. Health checks steer traffic away from bad pods.
Autoscaling changes how many backends exist — replica count on the vLLM Deployment, Ray Serve min_replicas / max_replicas, or GPU nodes when new pods cannot schedule.
Baseline deployment — infrastructure as code (Helm, Kustomize, Terraform): vLLM container, pinned model, nvidia.com/gpu request, probes, --max-num-seqs / --max-model-len from VRAM sizing.

Policy & thresholds — when a metric crosses a target for long enough, increase replicas; after a cooldown, decrease. Tooling: Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA) or Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) with Prometheus metrics; or Ray Serve autoscaling_config.
Placement — scheduler binds pods to GPU nodes. If none free, pods stay Pending; Cluster Autoscaler (CA) (GKE/EKS/AKS node pool autoscaler) adds machines — configured separately from pod autoscalers.

Admission — if scale-out is slow (cold start: pull image + load weights), the backend-for-frontend (BFF) or gateway returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests instead of unbounded queue — not autoscaling, but part of the same SLO story.
vLLM Deployment — minReplicas / maxReplicas (KEDA ScaledObject or HPA).
Ray Serve LLM deployment — min_replicas, max_replicas, target_ongoing_requests.
KubeRay worker group (optional) — minReplicas / maxReplicas on RayCluster worker pods when Ray needs more GPU slots.
GPU node pool — min / max node count and cloud GPU quota; cap Serve max_replicas to what you can schedule.
Agent Deployment — central processing unit (CPU) pool, its own HPA/KEDA; demand correlates with LLM calls but replica counts differ.
GPU inference — vLLM (memory-bound key-value (KV) cache + batching); scale on waiting queue, not GPU %.
CPU encoders — toxicity / decision transformers on Ray Serve or separate Deployments; scale on in-flight or R × LLM replicas from load tests.
Agent orchestration — LangGraph/FastAPI; scale on requests per second (RPS) / CPU; may colocate tiny models in-process.
Horizontal (scale out / in) — add vLLM pods or Ray Serve replicas behind the load balancer. Each replica is usually a full model copy (or one tensor parallel (TP) group = N GPUs in one pod).

Vertical (scale up / down) — bigger GPU SKU, TP across devices, or tune --max-num-seqs / quant / FP8 KV inside one replica. Kubernetes does not auto-resize GPU per pod; you change the Deployment template or node pool SKU.
Signal: vLLM num_requests_waiting (best leading indicator); or in-flight per pod vs target (Ray target_ongoing_requests). Use TTFT 95th percentile (p95) to validate SLOs, not as the only trigger.
Tooling: KEDA Prometheus trigger on waiting sum; HPA with Prometheus adapter; Ray Serve upscale_delay_s / downscale_delay_s (long downscale for LLM cold start).
Anti-pattern: HPA on GPU or CPU utilization alone — queue builds while utilization looks fine.
CronJob or GitOps schedule patches minReplicas on vLLM or GPU node pool min before daily peaks.
Ray: raise min_replicas before a known event (same idea as pre-warm in runbooks).
Hour-of-week baselines → higher minReplicas or warm GPU nodes.
Active users / sessions in Prometheus → KEDA scales min or gives early upscale (multiply by measured LLM-call rate per user).

Metadata per chunk: version, effective_date, status (active, superseded, retracted), supersedes (id of the replaced document), review_by, and the source authority tier.

Supersede on update. When a new version is indexed, mark the old chunks superseded (or delete them) in the same job. Queries filter to status = active; policy questions that depend on a date filter on effective_date.

Detect conflicts at ingest. Compare each new chunk with its nearest existing chunks from other sources or versions; flag pairs that are close in meaning but state different values (a window of 30 days against 90). Route flagged pairs to review or to a rule.

Resolve by rule, in this order: source authority (system of record over wiki over chat export), then effective date, then ingest time. If the rule cannot decide, keep both, label them with source and date, and escalate.
Expire what nobody owns. Documents past review_by are flagged or down-ranked until an owner re-confirms them.
At answer time, if retrieved chunks still disagree, the prompt tells the model to state the conflict and cite both sources instead of merging them. See conflicting chunks.
Measure it: index freshness lag (source change to searchable), count of active conflicts, and a conflict slice in the evaluation set (RAG evaluation).

Store metadata with each fact: subject (which user), attribute (employer, plan), value, source (user statement, tool result, model inference), timestamp, and confidence.
Update by key. Key facts by subject and attribute; a new value supersedes the old one. Keep the old value with validity dates only if history is needed.

Check for conflict on write. Memory is fetched at the start of each conversation anyway, so compare newly learned facts with the retrieved ones then. The most recent explicit statement from the user, or a tool result, beats an older or inferred value.

Set the lifetime by fact type. A time to live (TTL) per attribute: months for employer, minutes for plan tier, none for language preference. A single age cutoff deletes stable facts and keeps volatile ones too long.
Confirm instead of assuming when a fact is old and used for something visible or costly: “Are you still at Acme?”
Do not store what a tool can fetch. Plan, balance, and order status come from the system of record each time. If memory holds such a value anyway, tool results override it, and the prompt says so.
Record only established facts. A user's unverified claim (“my manager approved this”) is not a fact to save.

Isolate by subject. Write each fact under the authenticated user's id, take the id from the session rather than from the model, and filter on it before similarity search so one user's memory never reaches another (tenant filtering). Check the write path too: a colleague mentioned in a chat must not be saved as the user's own fact.
Support deletion on user request and keep personal data out of memory unless a feature needs it.
Short tasks, single session → working memory only + tight compaction.
Returning users / long projects → episodic + semantic stores with retrieval tool.
Large org knowledge → RAG corpus; agent memory holds session-specific residue only.
Repeated environment tasks → verified skill library before fine-tuning the base model.
Improve over time → pair memory with offline learning pipeline (learning & improvement).
